The catering.

premise: A man joins a gym in January, pays for the whole year up front, and walks to the treadmill for the first time in March.

premise: I moved closer to work to shorten my commute.

punchlines.text: Now I get there early enough to dread the whole day properly.
I saved forty minutes a day and spend every one of them staring at a wall I pay triple for.
The commute is nine minutes. The regret is ongoing.
I optimised for latency and completely forgot about cost.
I gained two hours a day and have used every single one of them lying down.

premise:

punchlines.text: "Non-zero."

"About as slim as the legroom you already paid for."

premise: Every company says it has an open-door policy.

The door is open. It is the calendar that is locked.
Mine really does. My manager is lovely. I simply have nothing to say to her.
Ours is so open that four hundred people have walked past it without ever going in.

premise: How many airline staff does it take to change a departure gate?

punchlines.text: Three: one to change the sign, one to change it back, and one to move the terminal six hundred feet while you sleep.
None. It changes itself, twice, while you are in the bathroom.
The number is not the joke. The walking is the joke.

premise: What's the difference between a city bus and a rumour?

punchlines.text: The rumour actually travels.
Both take forever to reach you, and then three of them show up at once.

premise: A man walks into his bank and asks to speak to somebody about his overdraft.

punchlines.text: They put him in a small room with a glass of water and a form headed "Options, Remaining".
The teller said the bank could not help, but the bank down the street has a lovely fountain he could reach into.
A man in a grey suit appeared, shook his hand, and congratulated him on being the bank's most reliable source of income.
They told him he was in the red, so he asked what they had in blue.

premise: I rang customer service about a parcel that was marked delivered but never arrived.

punchlines.text: They confirmed the parcel reached my address, my street, and my city, just not in that order.
They opened a case. The case is now older than the item I ordered.
The call lasted longer than this joke, and this joke is the only part I can shorten.
They said the driver marked it delivered, and that the driver no longer works there, and that those two facts are unrelated.
They asked if I had checked with my neighbours, and now my neighbours know exactly how many snacks I order.

premise:

punchlines.text: "Then give me a hundred and round up with feeling."

"Last season you gave me forty, and two of you gave up somewhere in the tunnel."

premise: Tax season is the one time of year when everybody becomes an accountant for six hours.

punchlines.text: And an expert in the six hours after that, when nothing can be changed.
I found two hundred in deductions and lost eleven hours finding them, so my hourly rate was insulting.
By hour four I had filed a sandwich from last March as a business development initiative.
For six hours a year we are all filing clerks, and then we file the whole thing away.

premise: Why do people say the gym is like a second home?

punchlines.text: Because you go in hoping for a longer life and come out a little closer to the end of one.
Nobody says that. People say the gym is expensive, and they are right.

premise: What's the difference between a hotel room and your own bedroom?

punchlines.text: In the hotel somebody makes the bed, and you still do not sleep.
One turns down your bed. The other turns down your requests.
One charges you for the Wi-Fi. The other charges your phone.

premise: A manager walks into a meeting fourteen minutes late, sits down, and says he only has ten minutes.

punchlines.text: He then spends nine of them explaining how busy he is.

Four hours later he is still talking, and the building has changed owners twice.
He leaves after his ten minutes, and the team spends fourteen deciding what he meant.
The rest of this joke was cut for time, which is the whole point.

premise: I asked the hotel front desk for a room with a view.

My window faces another window, and behind that one a man was also looking for a view.
They said the room overlooks the harbour. It certainly overlooked it.

premise: An airport is the only place where people will cheerfully pay nine dollars for a bottle of water.

punchlines.text: It is the one shop on earth where the customer has already decided not to argue.

premise: Why did the driver take the scenic route through the city centre at rush hour?

punchlines.text: He did not. The navigation app did, and it has never once apologised.

Because the motorway was closed. That is the whole reason. It was closed.
The app optimised for the shortest path, and the city optimised for the longest one.

premise: What's the difference between a sale and a clearance?

punchlines.text: In a sale the prices come down. In a clearance the shutters do.
In a sale the shop is doing well. In a clearance the shop is saying goodbye and hoping you do not notice.
Thirty percent.

premise: A woman moves to the city, buys a car on her first day, and drives it to work on her second.

punchlines.text: On the third day she sold the car and bought a bicycle, a helmet, and a very strong opinion about bike lanes.
She leaves it parked now and walks, because the parking space is worth more than the car.
The car is still out there. So is she. The lights have changed eleven times.
By the fourth day she took the train, which is what everyone told her on the first day.
She worked out her average speed for the week and found that her own walking pace had overtaken her.
